abstract: The ability for a subset of cells to establish a heterogeneous cell population with multi-lineage competency is crucial for the self-renewal capacity of tissues and organs. Restoration of heterogeneous gene expression patterns has been observed in pluripotent and multi-potent stem cells, and the heterogeneity restoration can influence the potential of differentiation into multiple cell types. Similarly, cancer cells can acquire the capacity to establish non-genetic heterogeneity that plays a role in cancer progression and resistance to therapeutics. Specific models of gene regulatory networks have been proposed to explain heterogeneity restoration. However, due to the lack of systematic analysis, it is unclear which network topologies are more efficient for this multicellular function, and what intrinsic and extrinsic factors can determine the optimal choice of network topology. In this work, we use mathematical models describing gene expression of single cells and their underlying population dynamics to examine the influence of network topology on the recovery of multimodal expression patterns originating from a homogeneous population. We found that feedback loops are a key factor contributing to heterogeneity restoration. Negative and positive feedback loops support the existence of heterogeneity restoration, but only positive feedback can accelerate the process with low cost of single-cell-level variations of expression. Furthermore, networks with mixed feedback were the most robust ones for heterogeneity restoration with respect to changes in both kinetic rate constants and noise levels. Using experimentally validated network databases, we showed that genes involved in feedback loops are enriched with functions related to cell fate decisions, and we identified examples of realistic gene regulatory networks cell fate dynamics. Our results suggest multiple potential evolutionary paths towards gene circuits governing heterogeneity restoration and key factors contributing to the dynamics of this process. We expect that this systematic study will enable future discoveries of new gene regulatory networks governing progenitor and cancer cell dynamics as well as therapeutic strategies targeting heterogeneity-enabling circuits.
